appraisal_events.evidence: M. de Charlus... tout entier livré à des goûts d'art; je fus stupéfait d'apprendre que c'était par lui qu'avait été peint l'immense éventail d'iris jaunes et noirs; J'ignorais absolument que le baron eût tous ces talents dont il ne parlait jamais.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's astonished discovery that Charlus is a genuinely accomplished, self-effacing artist (painter of the fan, composer of a sonatina) elevates him beyond his familiar role as mere brother-in-law and cousin.

appraisal_events.evidence: Ces stupides abréviations sont un signe de l'incompréhension que l'aristocratie a de sa propre poésie... il aurait voulu que son frère et sa belle-sœur disent de lui : « Charlus »; — Quel cachottier que ce Mémé... Avouez qu'il est drôle!... par moments un peu fou.
appraisal_events.explanation: Although Mme de Guermantes professes to adore Charlus and admire his rare worth, the family's habitual pet names and her closing teasing remarks ('cachottier', 'drôle', 'un peu fou') affectionately undercut the grand, princely self-image he wishes to project.

status_effects.explanation: Charlus comes off locally impressive because hidden artistic gifts are revealed that surprise the narrator and exceed the family's mundane view of him.
Charlus's desire to be addressed with unadorned princely simplicity ('Charlus' alone) is thwarted by his family's fond but reductive nicknames and teasing, denying him the grandeur he wants.

ambiguities: The diminishment in E2 blends the narrator's own ironic commentary on Charlus's vanity about nicknames with Mme de Guermantes's directly quoted teasing ('cachottier', 'un peu fou'); the two voices reinforce each other but are attributed to a single event for compression.
